notes.definition: When a reversible reaction occurs in a closed system, so that no reactants or products can escape, equilibrium is reached when the forward and reverse reactions occur at exactly the same rate.
explanation: A closed system is one where no substances can get in or out, for example a sealed flask. If a reversible reaction takes place in a closed system, none of the reactants or products can escape. This means the products are always there to react and reform the reactants, so the forward and reverse reactions can both keep happening. In an open container a gaseous product can escape, so the reverse reaction cannot keep up, and equilibrium is not reached.

At the start, there are only reactants, so the forward reaction is fast and the reverse reaction does not happen at all. As the reactants are used up their concentration falls, so the rate of the forward reaction decreases. At the same time, the concentration of the products increases, so the rate of the reverse reaction increases. Eventually the two rates become equal.

When the forward and reverse reactions are happening at exactly the same rate, the reaction has reached equilibrium. Products are being made at the same rate as they are being used up, so the amounts (and concentrations) of the reactants and products stay constant. This is sometimes called a dynamic equilibrium, because both reactions are still taking place; the reaction has not stopped.

It is important that the concentrations at equilibrium are constant, not equal. There might be much more product than reactant, or much more reactant than product, depending on the reaction and the conditions. On a graph of concentration against time, equilibrium is reached at the point where the lines for reactants and products become horizontal (flat).

You can see equilibrium in a sealed tube containing brown nitrogen dioxide gas, which forms colourless dinitrogen tetroxide: 2NO₂(g) ⇌ N₂O₄(g). Once equilibrium is reached, the colour of the gas stops changing, because nitrogen dioxide is being used up and made at the same rate. The colour does not show that the reactions have stopped, only that the amounts are constant.
keyFacts: Equilibrium can only be reached in a closed system, where no reactants or products can escape.
At equilibrium the forward and reverse reactions occur at exactly the same rate.
At equilibrium the amounts (concentrations) of reactants and products stay constant.
The concentrations at equilibrium are constant, but they are not usually equal.
At equilibrium both reactions are still happening: it is a dynamic equilibrium.
As the reaction proceeds, the forward rate decreases because the reactant concentration falls.
As products build up, the reverse rate increases.
On a concentration against time graph, equilibrium is reached when the lines become flat.
In an open container, gases can escape, so equilibrium cannot be reached.
Observable properties, such as colour, stop changing once equilibrium is reached.

keyTerms.definition: The state reached by a reversible reaction in a closed system when the forward and reverse reactions occur at exactly the same rate.
Apparatus that prevents the escape of reactants and products, and lets nothing else in, such as a sealed container.
An equilibrium in which the forward and reverse reactions are both still happening, at equal rates, so the amounts of substances stay constant.
The reaction from left to right in a reversible reaction equation.
The reaction from right to left in a reversible reaction equation.
The amount of a substance in a given volume; at equilibrium the concentrations of all substances stay constant.

workedExamples.title: Finding when equilibrium is reached
workedExamples.question: A reaction A ⇌ B is carried out in a sealed flask. The concentration of B (mol/dm³) is: 0 min: 0.00; 1 min: 0.30; 2 min: 0.48; 3 min: 0.58; 4 min: 0.62; 5 min: 0.62; 6 min: 0.62. When was equilibrium reached?
steps: At equilibrium the concentration of B stays constant.
The concentration stops changing at 0.62 mol/dm³.
It first reaches 0.62 mol/dm³ at 4 minutes and stays there.

workedExamples.title: Using a 1:1 equation
workedExamples.question: In the same reaction, the flask started with 1.00 mol/dm³ of A and no B. What is the concentration of A at equilibrium, and what percentage of A has been converted to B?
steps: The equation A ⇌ B is 1:1, so each mole of B formed uses one mole of A.
workedExamples.answer: 0.38 mol/dm³ of A; 62% converted. The concentrations are constant but not equal.

workedExamples.title: Rates at equilibrium
workedExamples.question: At equilibrium, the forward reaction of a system uses up nitrogen dioxide at a rate of 0.004 mol/dm³ per second. At what rate is nitrogen dioxide formed by the reverse reaction?
steps: At equilibrium the forward and reverse reactions occur at exactly the same rate.
So nitrogen dioxide is formed as fast as it is used up.
workedExamples.answer: 0.004 mol/dm³ per second, so the amount of nitrogen dioxide stays constant.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think that at equilibrium the concentrations of reactants and products are equal.
misconceptions.right: In fact the concentrations are constant, not equal. There may be much more of one than the other.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think that at equilibrium the reaction has stopped.
misconceptions.right: In fact both the forward and reverse reactions are still happening, at the same rate. That is why it is called a dynamic equilibrium.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think equilibrium can be reached in an open beaker.
misconceptions.right: In fact equilibrium needs a closed system. If a product escapes, it cannot take part in the reverse reaction.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think equilibrium means the rates of the forward and reverse reactions are zero.
misconceptions.right: In fact the rates are equal to each other, but not zero.

realWorld: In the Haber process, nitrogen and hydrogen react in a closed system and reach equilibrium, so only some of the reactants are converted to ammonia in each pass.
Fizzy drinks in a sealed bottle contain carbon dioxide at equilibrium with dissolved carbon dioxide; opening the bottle breaks the closed system and gas escapes.
In a sealed tube, brown nitrogen dioxide and colourless dinitrogen tetroxide reach an equilibrium mixture with a constant colour, which is often used to demonstrate equilibrium.
examTips: For the definition, give both points: a closed system, and the forward and reverse reactions occurring at exactly the same rate.
Never write that concentrations are 'equal' at equilibrium: write that they are 'constant' or 'do not change'.
If asked how a graph shows equilibrium, say the line becomes horizontal (flat), because the concentration no longer changes.
Explain changes in rate using concentration: as reactant concentration falls, the forward rate decreases; as product concentration rises, the reverse rate increases.
summary: Equilibrium can only be reached in a closed system.
At equilibrium the forward and reverse reactions occur at exactly the same rate.
Amounts of reactants and products stay constant at equilibrium, but are not usually equal.
Both reactions keep going: the equilibrium is dynamic.
Forward rate falls and reverse rate rises until they are equal.
Flat lines on a concentration against time graph show equilibrium.

flashcards.front: What is equilibrium in a reversible reaction?
flashcards.back: The state where the forward and reverse reactions occur at exactly the same rate.

flashcards.front: What type of system is needed for equilibrium?
flashcards.back: A closed system, where no reactants or products can escape.
Apparatus that prevents reactants and products escaping, and lets nothing else in (for example a sealed flask).

flashcards.front: What happens to the concentrations of reactants and products at equilibrium?
flashcards.back: They stay constant (they do not change).

flashcards.front: Are the concentrations of reactants and products equal at equilibrium?
flashcards.back: Not usually. They are constant, not equal.

flashcards.front: Has the reaction stopped at equilibrium?
flashcards.back: No. Both forward and reverse reactions continue at the same rate (dynamic equilibrium).

flashcards.front: Why does the forward rate decrease as a reaction approaches equilibrium?
flashcards.back: The concentration of reactants decreases, so there are fewer collisions per second.

flashcards.front: Why does the reverse rate increase as a reaction approaches equilibrium?
flashcards.back: The concentration of products increases, so they collide and react more often.

flashcards.front: How does a concentration against time graph show equilibrium?
Why can't equilibrium be reached in an open container with a gaseous product?
flashcards.back: The gas escapes, so it cannot take part in the reverse reaction.
The reactions are still happening, but the amounts of substances do not change.

flashcards.front: A sealed tube of NO₂ and N₂O₄ stops changing colour. What does this show?
flashcards.back: Equilibrium has been reached: NO₂ is used up and made at the same rate.

questions.question: In which type of system can a reversible reaction reach equilibrium?
markScheme: 1 mark: a closed system
questions.explanation: Equilibrium needs apparatus that prevents the escape of reactants and products. A catalyst or heating does not make equilibrium possible if substances can escape.
options: A system that is being heated

questions.question: Which statement is true for a reversible reaction at equilibrium?
markScheme: 1 mark: forward and reverse reactions occur at exactly the same rate
questions.explanation: At equilibrium both reactions continue at equal rates. Nothing has stopped.
options: The reverse reaction is faster than the forward reaction
The forward and reverse reactions occur at exactly the same rate

questions.question: Which of these is a closed system?
markScheme: 1 mark: a sealed flask
questions.explanation: A sealed flask prevents reactants and products escaping. The others are open to the air, so gases can escape.
options: A test tube with no bung

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows how the concentrations of a reactant and a product change during a reversible reaction in a closed system.
How can you tell from a graph like Figure 1 when equilibrium has been reached?
markScheme: 1 mark: the lines become horizontal
questions.explanation: At equilibrium the concentrations stay constant, so the lines become flat. Lines crossing only shows the concentrations are momentarily equal, which is not equilibrium.

questions.question: What happens to the concentrations of the reactants and products once a reaction has reached equilibrium?
markScheme: 1 mark: they stay constant
questions.explanation: Because the forward and reverse reactions occur at the same rate, substances are made as fast as they are used up, so concentrations stay constant. They are not usually equal.
options: They keep changing at the same rate

questions.question: At the very start of a reversible reaction, only reactants are present. Which statement is correct?
markScheme: 1 mark: forward rate highest, reverse rate zero
questions.explanation: With no products present, the reverse reaction cannot happen. The reactant concentration is greatest at the start, so the forward rate is greatest.
options: The forward rate is at its highest and the reverse rate is zero
The reverse rate is at its highest

questions.question:
Calcium carbonate is heated in an open crucible: CaCO₃(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO₂(g)
Why does this reaction not reach equilibrium?
markScheme: 1 mark: carbon dioxide escapes
questions.explanation: In an open crucible the carbon dioxide gas leaves, so it is not there to react with calcium oxide. Equilibrium needs a closed system.
options: Calcium oxide cannot react with anything
Carbon dioxide escapes, so the reverse reaction cannot keep pace

questions.question: Why is equilibrium in a closed system described as 'dynamic'?
markScheme: 1 mark: forward and reverse reactions are still happening
questions.explanation: Dynamic means active. Particles are still reacting in both directions, even though the overall amounts do not change.
options: Because the reaction moves in one direction only
Because the forward and reverse reactions are still happening

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows how the rates of the forward and reverse reactions change as a reversible reaction approaches equilibrium.
Why does the rate of the forward reaction decrease?
markScheme: 1 mark: reactant concentration decreases so fewer collisions per second
questions.explanation: As reactants are converted to products there are fewer reactant particles in the same volume, so collisions between them are less frequent.
options: The concentration of reactants decreases, so there are fewer successful collisions per second
The products block the reactant particles

questions.question:
A sealed tube contains brown nitrogen dioxide and colourless dinitrogen tetroxide at equilibrium: 2NO₂(g) ⇌ N₂O₄(g)
The colour stays the same. What is the best explanation?
markScheme: 1 mark: nitrogen dioxide used up and formed at the same rate
questions.explanation: The colour depends on the amount of brown NO₂. It stays constant because the forward and reverse reactions occur at the same rate, not because the reactions have stopped or the amounts are equal.
options: No more nitrogen dioxide is reacting
Nitrogen dioxide is being used up and formed at the same rate
All of the nitrogen dioxide has turned into dinitrogen tetroxide
There are equal amounts of nitrogen dioxide and dinitrogen tetroxide

questions.question:
The reaction A ⇌ B reaches equilibrium in a sealed flask.
Table 1 shows the concentrations at equilibrium. These values do not change.
A student says the reaction cannot be at equilibrium because the concentrations are different.
Which response is correct?
markScheme: 1 mark: student is wrong; concentrations are constant, not necessarily equal
questions.explanation: Equilibrium means the forward and reverse rates are equal, so concentrations stop changing. The values themselves can be very different.
options: The student is right: at equilibrium concentrations must be equal
The student is right: at equilibrium all of A must have reacted
The student is wrong: at equilibrium the concentrations are constant, not necessarily equal
The student is wrong: at equilibrium [A] must be greater than [B]

questions.question:
A reaction A ⇌ B is carried out in a sealed flask.
Table 1 shows how the concentration of B changes with time.
Determine the time when equilibrium was first reached.
markScheme: 1 mark: 4 minutes
questions.explanation: Equilibrium is reached when the concentration stops changing. [B] first reaches its constant value of 0.62 mol/dm³ at 4 minutes.

questions.question:
A reaction A ⇌ B is carried out in a sealed flask. The flask started with 1.00 mol/dm³ of A and no B. Each mole of B is formed from one mole of A.
Table 1 shows how the concentration of B changes with time.
Calculate the concentration of A at equilibrium.
markScheme: 1 mark: 0.38 mol/dm³
questions.explanation: The equation is 1:1, so the concentration of A that reacted equals the concentration of B formed: 0.62 mol/dm³. [A] = 1.00 − 0.62 = 0.38 mol/dm³.

questions.question:
A reaction A ⇌ B is carried out in a sealed flask. The flask started with 1.00 mol/dm³ of A and no B.
At equilibrium, the concentration of B is 0.62 mol/dm³.
Calculate the percentage of A converted into B at equilibrium.
markScheme: 1 mark: 62%
questions.explanation: Percentage converted = (amount reacted ÷ starting amount) × 100 = 0.62 ÷ 1.00 × 100 = 62%. The reaction does not go to completion because the reverse reaction also happens.

questions.question:
A reaction A ⇌ B is carried out in a sealed flask.
Table 1 shows how the concentration of B changes with time.
Calculate the mean rate of formation of B during the first 2 minutes.
markScheme: 1 mark: 0.24 mol/dm³ per min
questions.explanation: Mean rate = change in concentration ÷ time = (0.48 − 0.00) ÷ 2 = 0.24 mol/dm³ per min. The rate then slows as A is used up and the reverse reaction speeds up.

questions.question:
A system is at equilibrium in a sealed container. The forward reaction uses up substance X at a rate of 0.0035 mol/dm³ per second.
Determine the rate at which X is produced by the reverse reaction.
markScheme: 1 mark: 0.0035 mol/dm³ per s
questions.explanation: At equilibrium the forward and reverse reactions occur at exactly the same rate, so X is made as fast as it is used up. This is why the concentration of X stays constant.

questions.question: Describe what is meant by equilibrium for a reversible reaction.
markScheme: 1 mark: (in a closed system)
1 mark: forward and reverse reactions occur at the same rate
questions.explanation: Both points are needed for the full definition: the closed system and equal rates.
acceptedAnswers: forward and reverse reactions at the same rate

questions.question: State what is meant by a closed system.
markScheme: 1 mark: a system where no substances (reactants or products) can enter or leave
questions.explanation: A sealed container is a closed system. Gases cannot escape and air cannot get in.
acceptedAnswers: no reactants or products can escape
nothing can get in or out

questions.question:
A sealed tube contains a mixture of nitrogen dioxide (brown) and dinitrogen tetroxide (colourless). The mixture reaches equilibrium.
Describe what happens to the colour of the mixture once equilibrium is reached.
markScheme: 1 mark: the colour stays the same / stops changing
questions.explanation: At equilibrium the amount of brown nitrogen dioxide is constant, so the colour does not change.

questions.question: Explain why the concentrations of the reactants and products do not change at equilibrium, even though reactions are still happening.
markScheme: 1 mark: the forward and reverse reactions occur at the same rate
1 mark: so each substance is made as fast as it is used up
questions.explanation: The two reactions cancel each other out, so there is no overall change in amounts.
acceptedAnswers: forward and reverse at the same rate
products made as fast as they are used up

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows how the rates of the forward and reverse reactions change as a reversible reaction approaches equilibrium.
Explain why the rate of the reverse reaction increases.
markScheme: 1 mark: the concentration of products increases
1 mark: so product particles collide (and react) more often
questions.explanation: At the start there are no products. As they build up, the reverse reaction speeds up until it equals the forward rate.

questions.question: Ammonium chloride is heated in an open test tube with no bung. Suggest why the reaction does not reach equilibrium.
markScheme: 1 mark: not a closed system / ammonia and hydrogen chloride (gases) escape
1 mark: so the reverse reaction cannot occur at the same rate as the forward reaction
questions.explanation: Equilibrium needs both reactions to keep going at equal rates. If the products escape, the reverse reaction slows down or stops.

questions.question: A reaction reaches equilibrium in a closed system. Describe the shape of the line for the reactant and the line for the product on a graph of concentration against time.
markScheme: 1 mark: reactant concentration decreases (quickly at first), then becomes constant
1 mark: product concentration increases (from zero), then becomes constant
questions.explanation: Both lines become horizontal at the same time, when equilibrium is reached. They do not have to meet.

questions.question: Explain, in terms of rates and particles, how a reversible reaction in a closed system reaches equilibrium.
markScheme: 1 mark: reactant concentration falls so forward rate decreases (fewer collisions per second)
1 mark: product concentration rises so reverse rate increases
1 mark: eventually forward and reverse rates are equal, so equilibrium is reached
questions.explanation: Equilibrium is the point where the falling forward rate meets the rising reverse rate.

questions.question:
A student says: 'At equilibrium there must be 50% reactants and 50% products.'
Explain why the student is wrong.
markScheme: 1 mark: at equilibrium the amounts are constant (not necessarily equal)
1 mark: the proportions depend on the reaction (and conditions); equilibrium only requires equal rates
questions.explanation: Equilibrium is about equal rates of reaction, not equal amounts.
acceptedAnswers: depends on the reaction and conditions

questions.question:
Hydrogen and iodine are sealed in a flask and heated: H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g)
Describe how the rates of the forward and reverse reactions, and the amounts of each substance, change from the start until equilibrium is reached.
markScheme: Indicative content: at the start only hydrogen and iodine are present; the forward rate is at its highest and the reverse rate is zero; as hydrogen and iodine are used up, their concentrations decrease and the forward rate decreases; hydrogen iodide is formed and its concentration increases; the reverse rate increases; eventually the forward and reverse rates are equal; equilibrium is reached; amounts of H₂, I₂ and HI then stay constant (but are not equal); both reactions continue.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a clear description of how both rates and the amounts change, ending in a correct description of equilibrium.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements about rates or amounts, with limited sequencing.
questions.explanation: Describe both rates and the amounts of substances, in order from the start to equilibrium.

questions.question:
Evaluate these three statements about a reversible reaction at equilibrium in a closed system:
1. 'The reaction has stopped.'
2. 'The amounts of reactants and products are constant.'
3. 'The concentrations of reactants and products are equal.'
markScheme: Indicative content: statement 1 is incorrect: both the forward and reverse reactions continue (dynamic equilibrium); statement 2 is correct: because the forward and reverse rates are equal, each substance is made as fast as it is used up; statement 3 is incorrect: the concentrations are constant but usually different, depending on the reaction and conditions; equilibrium is defined by equal rates, not equal amounts.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): all three statements correctly judged with clear reasons linked to equal rates.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): one or two statements correctly judged with limited reasons.
questions.explanation: For each statement say whether it is correct, then explain using the idea that the rates are equal.

questions.question:
Hydrogen (colourless) and iodine gas (purple) are sealed in a flask and heated. They react to form hydrogen iodide (colourless):
H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g)
The purple colour fades at first, then stays a constant pale purple.
Explain these observations. Use ideas about rates, concentrations and equilibrium.
markScheme: Indicative content: at the start there is a high concentration of iodine, so the mixture is purple; hydrogen and iodine react to form colourless hydrogen iodide; the concentration of iodine decreases, so the purple colour fades; the forward rate decreases because the reactant concentrations decrease (fewer collisions per second); as hydrogen iodide builds up, the reverse reaction (2HI → H₂ + I₂) speeds up, reforming iodine; the flask is sealed, so it is a closed system and no substances escape; eventually the forward and reverse rates are equal; equilibrium is reached; iodine is used up and formed at the same rate, so its concentration is constant and the colour stays the same; the colour is pale purple, not colourless, because the reaction does not go to completion: some iodine remains at equilibrium; the reactions have not stopped (dynamic equilibrium).
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a detailed, logical explanation linking the colour changes to iodine concentration, the changing rates of both reactions, the closed system and dynamic equilibrium.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): explains the fading colour and describes equilibrium as equal rates, with some link to constant colour.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements, for example 'the iodine reacts so the colour fades', with little explanation.
questions.explanation: The colour tracks the concentration of iodine. It stops changing because iodine is used up and made at equal rates once equilibrium is reached.
